title: Follow geometry through a graphics pipeline
summary: Separate vertex work, rasterization and fragment outcomes.
objectives: Assign work to vertex processing, rasterization and fragment processing.
Explain why a generated fragment is not a guaranteed framebuffer write.

blocks.title: Prerequisites and subject boundary
blocks.text: Prerequisites: C++ resource concepts and two-dimensional coordinates. This unit owns rendering and GPU concepts; C++ containers and RAII only organize the host-side implementation.

A graphics pipeline turns geometry and state into potential image updates. In the conventional primitive-shading path described by Vulkan, vertices form primitives, vertex shaders compute positions and attributes, and later processing clips and rasterizes primitives. Rasterization generates fragments associated with framebuffer regions. Fragment shading and tests then determine which values reach attachments. A vertex is therefore not a pixel, and a fragment is not a promise that a visible pixel will change. Different pipeline stages operate over different kinds of input. Keeping those roles separate helps diagnose whether a missing object originates in geometry, transformation, coverage, testing or output configuration.

Begin with the question each stage answers. Vertex processing determines transformed positions and attributes. Primitive processing organizes geometry. Rasterization determines potential covered locations according to the configured rules. Fragment processing calculates candidate values and applies relevant operations before attachment updates. The order described here is a conceptual reasoning path; actual shader and test execution can be constrained or optimized according to the specification.

Coordinates need a stated space. A local-space point describes geometry relative to its object. A transformed point describes it in the destination of the chosen transformation. Our two-dimensional addition is only a mathematical stand-in for vertex transformation; it is not a complete Vulkan clip-space setup. Omitting projection deliberately avoids treating arbitrary local coordinates as immediately valid framebuffer locations.

A vertex attribute and a fragment value have different multiplicities. A triangle has three vertices, yet may cover many samples, few samples or none. Conversely a fragment's candidate color may fail a configured test or be combined with an existing attachment value. Counting vertex invocations cannot tell you the final number of visible pixels. Debugging should inspect an intermediate contract at the stage where the relevant quantity exists.

Treat pipeline state as part of the input. Geometry alone does not define the picture; shader interfaces, attachments and enabled tests also matter. A useful controlled experiment fixes these settings and changes one suspected cause at a time. If translation, culling and output attachment selection all change together, a newly visible triangle does not identify which earlier condition prevented the write.

blocks.prompt: Translate vertices (0,0), (2,0) and (0,2) by (-1,0) in the same coordinate system. Which facts can you conclude without specifying the rest of the pipeline?
blocks.explanation: The new coordinates are (-1,0), (1,0) and (-1,2). Translation preserves their pairwise displacements, so the triangle's shape is unchanged in this coordinate model. You cannot infer exact framebuffer coverage, clipping or final color from those values alone because the projection, viewport and other state were deliberately omitted.

parts.title: Trace transformation and contrasting depth outcomes

blocks.text: Use a conceptual two-dimensional triangle with local vertices (0,0), (2,0) and (0,2). For this exercise the vertex transformation translates x by one and y by two. We deliberately omit projection, clipping conventions and API setup. The rasterizer is assumed to generate a particular interior fragment, and a configured depth test can accept or reject it.

blocks.caption: Original worked trace; finite assumptions, not executable platform code
blocks.code:
Local triangle:       (0,0), (2,0), (0,2)
After translation:   (1,2), (3,2), (1,4)
Rasterization:       produce an interior fragment F
Fragment shading:   candidate color for F = blue
Depth test passes:  blue may be written, subject to other configured operations
Depth test fails:   F contributes no color write in this example

blocks.text: The three transformed coordinates describe geometry; they do not enumerate every affected sample. An object can have valid vertices yet disappear because a later test rejects its fragments. The example uses translation so that each coordinate is easy to verify, rather than hiding the stage distinction inside matrix notation. Real Vulkan setup also specifies attachments, shader interfaces and other state. Those contracts must agree with the data supplied by the application.

Translation adds the same vector to each point: (0,0)+(1,2)=(1,2), (2,0)+(1,2)=(3,2), and (0,2)+(1,2)=(1,4). The relative edge vectors remain (2,0) and (0,2), so the geometry's shape is preserved in this mathematical exercise. That arithmetic checks transformation only; it does not establish coverage under omitted projection and rasterization rules.

The trace then stipulates an interior fragment F. Its candidate blue color is a value to be considered by later configured operations. The two depth outcomes compare what happens to that same candidate under different test results. If the test fails, this example makes no color write for F. If it passes, the remaining operations still have to permit the intended update.

blocks.title: Trace transformation and contrasting depth outcomes
blocks.text: Contrasting diagnostic model: stipulate an opaque red attachment initially, blending disabled, color writes enabled, and a simple LESS depth test. The existing depth at F is 0.4.

With candidate depth 0.6, the comparison 0.6 < 0.4 is false. The modeled fragment fails and the stored color stays red. Change only the candidate depth to 0.3. Now 0.3 < 0.4 is true; assuming all other configured conditions permit the write, blue replaces red. This is a finite hypothetical test, not a measurement or a claim about every depth configuration.

Now disable the color write while retaining the passing depth comparison. The triangle can still generate the stipulated fragment and pass the modeled test without changing the color attachment. The visible symptom resembles the earlier failure, but the responsible contract differs. A diagnostic sequence should therefore check coverage, tests and enabled writes separately instead of treating every unchanged pixel as a vertex-shader problem.

blocks.prompt: Under the second scenario's LESS comparison, what happens at candidate depth 0.4, and why must the comparison name be recorded?
blocks.explanation: Equality does not satisfy LESS, so 0.4 < 0.4 is false and the modeled fragment fails. A less-than-or-equal configuration would give a different result. Recording only that depth testing is enabled omits a behaviorally important setting. The numeric test is original arithmetic under a stated configuration, not a universal rule that equal-depth fragments always disappear.

blocks.text: Change the translation to minus one in x and keep y unchanged. Compute all three new vertices before thinking about shading. Then devise a diagnostic sequence: inspect transformed geometry, inspect coverage, and inspect relevant tests and writes. Avoid changing unrelated pipeline state all at once. A small known triangle with a simple output is a more interpretable experiment than a full scene containing many assets and materials.

blocks.prompt: If the vertex shader runs successfully, does that prove the triangle appears in the final image?
blocks.explanation: No. Successful vertex processing only establishes one stage of the path. Clipping, rasterization coverage, depth or stencil decisions, attachment configuration and later operations can affect the result. The pipeline model tells you which intermediate fact to inspect next rather than treating rendering as one indivisible operation.

blocks.text: A rendering explanation should connect each observed result to the stage and state that governs it. Verify coordinates mathematically, establish coverage under the actual pipeline, and inspect tests and attachment operations before concluding that output must change. Carry this approach into textures, lighting and larger scenes; each additional stage introduces another input contract that can be checked independently.
